en: Sukeśa Bhāradvāja, Śaibya Satyakāma, Sauriyāyaṇī Gārgya, Kausalya Āśvalāyana,

Bhārgava Vaidarbhi, and Kabandhī Kātyāyana— these, devoted to Brahman, grounded in Brahman, seeking the Supreme Brahman, thinking, "He indeed will tell us all that," approached the venerable Pippalāda with fuel in their hands. (PrU 1.1)
That seer said to them:
"Dwell for another year with austerity, celibacy, and faith;
then ask questions as you desire."
"If we know it all, we shall tell you everything. // PrUp 1.2 //
Then Kabandhī Kātyāyana approached and asked:
"Venerable sir, from what indeed are these creatures born? (PrU 1.3)
To him he said:
"Prajāpati, desiring offspring, performed austerity."
Having performed austerity, he produced a pair: wealth and breath, thinking, "These two shall produce offspring for me in many ways. (PrU 1.4)
The breath, indeed, is the sun; the moon is wealth (rayi).
Wealth, indeed, is all this that is both formed and formless;
therefore, form itself is wealth.
Now, as the sun rises and enters the eastern quarter, by that he deposits the eastern vital breaths within his rays.
As he illuminates the south, the west, the north, what is below, what is above, the intermediate directions, and everything—all that—by that he deposits all the vital breaths within his rays.

This very Vaiśvānara, the universal-formed breath, rises as fire; concerning this, this has been declared by Dakṣa: PrUp_1.7: "The sun is the honey of the gods; its eastern rays are the eastern honey-cells. The Ṛg-verses are the bees; the Ṛg-verses produce the honey. PrUp_1.7: "That which is the brilliance of the sun is the honey; that which is its white [light] is the flower; that which is its heat is the seed. PrUp_1.7: "From that, the Ṛg-verses flow forth; from that, the Sāman-chants flow forth; from that, the Yajus-formulas flow forth; from that, indeed, all these beings flow forth. PrUp_1.7: "By that, indeed, the gods live; by that, humans live; by that, the fathers live; by that, the beasts live; by that, everything here lives—whatever there is, whether moving or breathing, or whatever is not moving and does not breathe. This is the honey of the gods. PrUp_1.7: "He who knows this thus becomes a honey-maker among the gods; he becomes a honey-maker among kings; he becomes a honey-maker among the people; he becomes a honey-maker among the cattle-herders; he becomes a honey-maker among his own kin; he becomes a honey-maker among those with whom he comes into contact. He becomes a possessor of food, an eater of food. He reaches the full span of life, whoever knows this thus. PrUp_1.7: "Now, its southern rays are the southern honey-cells. The Yajus-formulas are the bees; the Yajus-formulas produce the honey. PrUp_1.7: "That which is the brilliance of the sun is the honey; that which is its white [light] is the flower; that which is its heat is the seed. The Sāman-chants are the bees; the Sāman-chants produce the honey. The Atharva-Aṅgiras verses are the bees; the Atharva-Aṅgiras verses produce the honey. PrUp_1.7: "That which is the brilliance of the sun is the honey; that which is its white [light] is the flower; that which is its heat is the seed. PrUp_1.7: "From that, the Atharva-Aṅgiras verses flow forth; from that, the Itihāsas and Purāṇas flow forth; from that, the Gāthās and Nārāśaṃsīs flow forth; from that, indeed, all these beings flow forth. This is the honey of the gods. He becomes a possessor of food, an eater of food. He reaches the full span of life, whoever knows this thus. PrUp_1.7: "Now, its upward rays are the upper honey-cells. The Upaniṣads are the bees; the Upaniṣads produce the honey. The secret doctrine (Upaniṣad) is the bee; the secret doctrine produces the honey. PrUp_1.7: "That which is the brilliance of the sun is the honey; that which is its white [light] is the flower; that which is its heat is the seed. For it is the honey of all beings. Truly, he who knows this thus becomes a honey-maker among the gods; he becomes a honey-maker among kings; he becomes a honey-maker among the people; he becomes a honey-maker among the cattle-herders; he becomes a honey-maker among his
The omniform, golden-hued Jātavedas, the ultimate resort, the one light that blazes—this Sun, the breath of all creatures, rises with a thousand rays, manifesting itself in a hundred ways. (PrU 1.8)
The year, indeed, is Prajāpati.
Its two courses are the southern and the northern.
Now, those who meditate upon that as "the performance of sacrifices and works of public utility" (iṣṭāpūrta) win only the world of the moon.
They indeed return again.
Therefore, these seers, desiring offspring, proceed along the southern path;
for this path of the fathers is indeed wealth.
Then, having sought the Self through austerity, celibacy, faith, and knowledge, they conquer the sun.
This, indeed, is the abode of the vital breaths; this is the immortal; this is the ultimate goal.
From this, they do not return again.
This is cessation. Regarding this, there is the following verse: PrUp 1.10.
They say that the Father has five feet and twelve forms, abounding in moisture in the further half of heaven;
but others say that He is the far-seeing One, established upon a seven-wheeled, six-spoked chariot. 1.11.

The month, indeed, is Prajāpati; its dark fortnight is his wealth (rayi), and its bright fortnight is his vital breath (prāṇa). Therefore, these seers perform sacrifices during the bright fortnight, while others do so during the other.
Prajāpati is indeed day and night;
his day is breath and his night is wealth.
Those who unite with sexual pleasure during the day surely cast their breath away.
That which they unite with in passion during the night is indeed the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya).
Food, indeed, is Prajāpati; from that, verily, comes semen;
from that these creatures are born. (PrU 1.14)
Therefore, those who indeed observe that vow of Prajāpati produce a pair;
for them alone is this world of Brahman.
In whom austerity and celibacy reside,
and in whom truth is firmly established.
For those in whom there is no falsehood of the tongue and no deceit, that dustless world of Brahman belongs. (PrU 1.16)
Therefore, Bhārgava Vaidarbhi asked him:
"Venerable sir, how many gods indeed sustain created beings?
Which among them illuminate this?"
But which among these is the most excellent? (PrU 2.1)
To him he said:
"This god is indeed space—wind, fire, water, earth, speech, mind, sight, and hearing.
Having manifested themselves, they speak."
We support this arrow by holding it steady. (PrUp 2.2)
The most excellent Prāṇa said to them:
"Do not fall into delusion;
it is I alone who, having divided myself fivefold, support and sustain this body."
They became lacking in faith.
Due to that conceit, it seems to ascend upward;
when it ascends, all the others indeed ascend;
and when it settles down, all the others indeed settle down.
Just as when the king of bees departs, all the bees depart together,
and when he settles down, they all settle down together;
so it is with speech, mind, sight, and hearing.
Being delighted, they praise the vital breath (prāṇa).
This is Agni; this is Sūrya; this is Parjanya, the Maghavan; this is Vāyu;
this is the Earth, Rayi, and the God; this is that which exists and does not exist, and that which is immortal. (PrU 2.5)
As the spokes are fixed in the nave of a wheel, everything is established in the vital breath (prāṇa):
the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, the sacrifice, the ruling power (kṣatra), and the spiritual power (brahman).
O Prāṇa, you move about as Prajāpati within the womb; you alone are born again.
To you these creatures bring tribute, O Prāṇa, you who are established through the vital breaths.
You are the foremost bearer of offerings for the gods; you are the first *svadhā* for the ancestors;
you are the truth practiced by the seers, and you belong to the Atharvans and Aṅgirases.
O Prāṇa, you are Indra by your splendor; you are Rudra when withdrawing the world;
and you are the protector, the guardian, and the preserver who protects it entirely on all sides during its maintenance, through your gentle form.
You move incessantly in the intermediate space; as the sun, you alone are the lord of all lights through your rising and setting.
But when you rain down, O Prāṇa, these creatures of yours abide in a state of bliss, thinking, "Food shall come according to our desire. (PrU 2.10)
O Prāṇa, you are the Vrātya, the sole seer, the eater, the true lord of all;
we are the givers for you, and you, O Mātariśvan, are our father.
That form of yours which is established in speech, that which is in the ear and that which is in the eye, and that which is continuous in the mind—make that auspicious; do not depart.
"All this, whatever is established in the third heaven, is under the control of the vital breath (prāṇa).
Protect us like a mother her sons, and bestow upon us prosperity and wisdom. (PrU 2.13)
Then Kausalya Āśvalāyana questioned him:
"Venerable sir, from where is this vital breath born?
How does it enter this body?"
Or, having divided itself, how does it establish itself? By what means does it depart?
How does it designate the external?
"What is meant by 'within'? (PrU 3.1)
To him he said:
"You ask questions that go too far;
you are one who has reached the highest in Brahman."
Therefore, I shall speak to you. PrUp 3.2.
This vital breath is born from the self;
just as this shadow is extended upon a person, so is that [breath] extended upon this [self];
through the action of the mind, it enters into this body.
Just as a sovereign king appoints his officials,
saying, "Rule over these villages, rule over those villages," even so does this vital breath (prāṇa) assign the other vital breaths each to their respective places.
Apāna is located in the anus and the generative organ;
Prāṇa itself is established in the eyes, ears, mouth, and nostrils;
while Samāna resides in the middle.
For he indeed leads this offered food equally;
therefore, these become the seven flames.
For this Self is in the heart;
here there are one hundred and one channels,
and from each of these there are a hundred branches.
There are seventy-two thousand secondary branch-nerves;
in these the vyāna breath moves.
Then, by means of the upward-moving *udāna* alone, he leads [the self] through merit to the world of merit, through evil to the world of evil,
and by both together to the world of men.
The sun indeed rises as the external breath,
for it supports this very breath of the eye.
That deity which is in the earth, she, having taken hold of the downward breath (apāna) of the person—
That which is space in between is the *samāna* breath;
the wind is the *vyāna*.
The udāna is indeed heat;
therefore, one whose heat has subsided [does not depart],
as he attains a new existence through the senses merging into the mind.
By that mind, this [self] enters into the vital breath;
the vital breath, joined with heat, together with the self, leads it to the world as it has been conceived.
He who, knowing this, knows the vital breath—his offspring does not perish, and he becomes immortal. Regarding this, there is this verse: Prasna Upanishad 3.11.

Having understood the fivefold nature of the vital breath—its origin, its arrival, its location, its pervasiveness, and its internal state—one attains the immortal; having understood it, one attains the immortal. Thus ends the third chapter, section twelve.
Then Sauryāyaṇī Gārgya questioned him:
"Venerable sir, in this person, what things sleep?
What things remain awake here?"
"Which god is it that sees dreams? To whom does this pleasure belong? Upon what, indeed, are all things established? (PrU 4.1)
To him he said:
"Just as, Gārgya, when the sun is setting, all its rays become unified in this orb of light,
and they spread out again and again when it rises."
In this very way, indeed, all that becomes unified in the supreme deity, the mind.
Therefore, at that time, this person does not hear;
he does not see.
He does not smell; he does not taste; he does not touch.
He does not greet;
he does not accept;
he does not take pleasure.
He does not emit, he does not inhale;
they say that he sleeps. 4.2.
In this city, the fires of the vital breaths indeed remain awake.
The apāna is the gārhapatya fire;
the vyāna is the anvāhāryapacana fire.
That which is led forth from the Gārhapatya fire by means of the leading-forth (praṇayana) is the Āhavanīya; it is the vital breath (prāṇa).
That which carries these two oblations—the inhalation and the exhalation—equally is the *samāna*.
The mind, indeed, is the sacrificer;
the fruit of the sacrifice is the *udāna*.
Day after day, it leads this sacrificer to Brahman.
In this state, this deity experiences its own majesty in a dream:
it beholds what was seen and what was desired;
it hears again the very meaning of what was heard.
And he repeatedly experiences again what has been experienced in various countries and distant regions.
He sees everything—what was seen and what was not seen, what was heard and what was not heard, what was experienced and what was not experienced, what is real and what is unreal.
When he is overcome by light,
then this deity does not see dreams;
then, in this body, there is this bliss.
Just as, my dear, birds settle upon a tree for shelter,
even so, indeed, all this settles in the supreme Self.
Earth and the mere element of earth; water and the mere element of water;
fire and the mere element of fire.
Wind and the wind-element; space and the space-element;
the eye and the visible object.
The ear and that which is to be heard; the nose and that which is to be smelled; the tongue and that which is to be tasted.
The skin and that which is to be touched;
the voice and that which is to be spoken; the hands and that which is to be grasped.
The generative organ and that which is to be brought to pleasure; the anus and that which is to be discharged;
and the feet and that which is to be traversed.
The mind and the object of thought;
the intellect and the object of cognition; the ego-sense and the object of the ego-sense.
The mind and that which is to be willed; fire and that which is to be illumined; breath and that which is to be sustained. PrUp 4.8.
For this person— the self consisting of consciousness, the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower, and the agent—
is established in the supreme imperishable Self.
He attains the supreme Imperishable itself.
O dear one, he who knows that shadowless, bodiless, bloodless, radiant Imperishable—
he, being all, becomes everything.
Regarding this, there is the following verse: PrUp 4.10.

"O gentle one, he who knows that imperishable wherein the conscious self, along with all the gods, the vital breaths, and all beings are established—he is all-knowing; indeed, he has entered into everything. (PrU 4.11)
Then Śaibya Satyakāma questioned him:
"Venerable sir, if someone among men should meditate upon the syllable *oṃ* until the end of his life,
which world indeed does he win by that?"
To him he said:
"Satyakāma, this syllable Om is indeed the higher and the lower Brahman.
Therefore, the knower, by means of this very support, attains one or the other. (PrUp 5.2)
If he meditates on it as consisting of a single measure,
being made conscious by that very [measure], he immediately reaches the earth;
the *Ṛg* verses lead him to the world of men.
Endowed there with austerity, celibacy, and faith, he experiences greatness.
Now, if he attains the mind by means of the two measures,
he is led up to the intermediate space by the Yajus formulas to the world of Soma.
Having experienced splendor in the world of Soma, he returns again.
Furthermore, he who meditates upon the Supreme Person by means of this very syllable "Om" consisting of three measures,
having merged with the heat in the sun,
is liberated like a snake from its slough.

Thus, indeed, released from evil, he is led up by the Sāmans to the world of Brahman. From this mass of living beings, he beholds the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the high. On this subject there are these two verses: Prasna Upanishad 5.5.1–2: The Person of the size of a thumb dwells in the heart of beings; He is the lord of the past and the future, and therefore He does not perish after death. I know Him as the great omnipresent One; Therefore, I am immortal, O Maitreyī. So I believe. When a man has departed, his speech merges into fire, His breath into wind, His sight into the sun, His mind into the moon, His hearing into the quarters, His body into the earth, His self (ātman) into the space, And his senses, having reached the ether, merge into that [ether]. Now, when a man departs from here, there is no consciousness for him. They say: "He has become one with the heat. "No," said Śākalya, "it is not so. Just as a caterpillar, having reached the tip of a blade of grass, draws itself together toward it to take hold of it, even so this Self, having cast off this body and dispelled ignorance, draws itself together to take hold of the intellect (vijñāna). Or, as a weaver, having removed a finished cloth, weaves another—newer and more beautiful—one, even so this Self, having cast off this body and dispelled ignorance, attains a form that is newer and more beautiful, whether it be like that of the ancestors, or like that of the Gandharvas, or like that of the gods, or like that of Prajāpati, or like that of Brahmā, or else like that of other beings. This very Self is That which has been described as 'Not this, not this' (neti neti), which is incomprehensible because it is beyond comprehension, and which is imperishable because all qualities of perishability have been discarded. There is no diversity here at all. He who perceives diversity goes from death to death. "Then, what is it that remains? "It is the unmanifest and the manifest, the defined and the undefined, the mortal and the immortal, the stationary and the moving. It is both the real and the unreal. But by means of the Real alone, one attains the Real. A person consists of desire. As is his desire, so is his resolve; as is his resolve, so is the action he performs; and whatever action he performs, that he comes to be. On this point, there are these verses: One who desires the worlds of the fathers through ritual acts, Is born among the fathers by those very acts. But one who desires the worlds of the mothers through austerity, Is born among the mothers by that very austerity. One who is desirous of becoming many, Through meditation and through fervor, Enters into the womb, To be born again in manifold forms. But one who is without desire, whose desire is stilled, Whose desire is the Self, Dissolves away into the elements, And does not come into being again. The fire becomes his fire, The fuel becomes his fuel, The smoke becomes his smoke, The flame becomes his flame, The coals become his coals, The sparks become his sparks. In this manner, a knower of yoga, absorbed in yoga, Reaches the deity of fire and, from there, reaches the deity of day. From the deity of day, he reaches the deity of the waxing fortnight, And from the northern course of the sun, he reaches the year. From the year, he reaches the sun, And from the sun, he reaches the moon. From the moon, he reaches the lightning. There, a being who is not human leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods. Those who follow the path of sacrifice and charity, As well as those who practice austerity in the forest, Reach the smoke, and from the smoke, the night, From the night, the dark fortnight, And from the dark fortnight, the southern course of the sun. Having reached the year from the southern course, They proceed by the same path as before. These two paths are indeed the great roadways of the world. By one of them, people go upward, And by the other, they return downward. He who does not belong to these two paths Becomes a mere creature of the cycle of rebirth. Wandering back and forth between these two worlds, He fails to realize the bliss of the eternal Brahman. Thus, indeed, released from evil, he is led up by the Sāmans to the world of Brahman. From this mass of living beings, he beholds the Person dwelling in the city, who is higher than the high. On this subject there are these two verses: The Person of the size of a thumb dwells in the heart of beings; He is the lord of the past and the future, and therefore He does not perish after death. I know Him as the great omnipresent One; Therefore, I am immortal, O Maitreyī. So I believe. When a man has departed, his speech merges into fire, His breath into wind, His sight into the sun, His mind into the moon, His hearing into the quarters, His body into the earth, His self (ātman) into the space, And his senses, having reached the ether, merge into that [ether]. Now, when a man departs from here, there is no consciousness for him. They say: "He has become one with the heat. "No," said Śākalya, "it is not so. Just as a caterpillar, having reached the tip of a blade of grass, draws itself together toward it to take hold of it, even so this Self, having cast off this body and dispelled ignorance, draws itself together to take hold of the intellect (vijñāna). Or, as a weaver, having removed a finished cloth, weaves another—newer and more beautiful—one, even so this Self, having cast off this body and dispelled ignorance, attains a form that is newer and more beautiful, whether it be like that of the ancestors, or like that of the Gandharvas, or like that of the gods, or like that of Prajāpati, or like that of Brahmā, or else like that of other beings. This very Self is That which has been described as 'Not this, not this' (neti neti), which is incomprehensible because it is beyond comprehension, and which is imperishable because all qualities of perishability have been discarded. There is no diversity here at all. He who perceives diversity goes from death to death. "Then, what is it that remains? "It is the unmanifest and the manifest, the defined and the undefined, the mortal and the immortal, the stationary and the moving. It is both the real and the unreal. But by means of the Real alone, one attains the Real. A person consists of desire. As is his desire, so is his resolve; as is his resolve, so is the action he performs; and whatever action he performs, that he comes to be. On this point, there are these verses: One who desires the worlds of the fathers through ritual acts, Is born among the fathers by those very acts. But one who desires the worlds of the mothers through austerity, Is born among the mothers by that very austerity. One who is desirous of becoming many, Through meditation and through fervor, Enters into the womb, To be born again in manifold forms. But one who is without desire, whose desire is stilled, Whose desire is the Self, Dissolves away into the elements, And does not come into being again. The fire becomes his fire, The fuel becomes his fuel, The smoke becomes his smoke, The flame becomes his flame, The coals become his coals, The sparks become his sparks. In this manner, a knower of yoga, absorbed in yoga, Reaches the deity of fire and, from there, reaches the deity of day. From the deity of day, he reaches the deity of the waxing fortnight, And from the northern course of the sun, he reaches the year. From the year, he reaches the sun, And from the sun, he reaches the moon. From the moon, he reaches the lightning. There, a being who is not human leads them to Brahman. This is the path of the gods. Those who follow the path of sacrifice and charity, As well as those who practice austerity in the forest, Reach the smoke, and from the smoke, the night, From the night, the dark fortnight, And from the dark fortnight, the southern course of the sun. Having reached the year from the southern course, They proceed by the same path as before. These two paths are indeed the great roadways of the world. By one of them, people go upward, And by the other, they return downward.
Three measures, subject to death, are employed, joined one to another and not separated:
when these are correctly applied in external, internal, and intermediate actions, the knower does not tremble. (PrUp 5.6)

With the *ṛg*-verses this [world], with the *yajus*-formulas the intermediate space, and that which the seers know through the *sāman*-chants—he who knows follows that which is peaceful, undecaying, immortal, fearless, and supreme, by means of the *oṃ* syllable as his very abode. (PrU 5.7)
Then Sukeśa Bhāradvāja asked him:
"Venerable sir, Prince Hiraṇyanābha of Kosala approached me and asked this question:
'O Bhāradvāja, do you know the Person consisting of sixteen parts?'"
I said to that youth, "I do not know this.
If I had known it, why would I not have told you?
Indeed, he who speaks untruth withers away, root and all."
"Therefore, I ought not to speak a falsehood.
He mounted his chariot in silence and departed.
To him he said:
"Right here within the body, my dear, is that person in whom these sixteen parts originate."
He reflected:
"When I have departed, in what shall I depart? Or when I am established, in what shall I be established? PrU 6.3.
He created vital breath.
From vital breath, he created faith, space, air, light, water, earth, the senses, mind, food; from food, vigor, austerity, sacred formulas, action, worlds, and within the worlds, name.
Just as these rivers, flowing toward the ocean, reach the ocean and vanish;
their names and forms are destroyed,
and they are simply called "the ocean."
In the same way, these sixteen parts of this observer, which have the Puruṣa as their goal, reach the Puruṣa and dissolve away;
their name and form are split apart,
and they are called simply "Puruṣa."

He becomes partless and immortal; regarding this, there is this verse: Prasna Upanishad 6.5.1–2: The one who knows thus becomes Brahman, the life of lives, the eye of eyes, the ear of ears, the food of foods, the mind of minds. The wise ones, having known this, depart from here as those who have become Brahman. "He who knows that Puruṣa to be known—in whom, as in the nave of a wheel, all parts are established—may death not afflict you. (PrU 6.6)
He said to them:
"This much indeed I know of that supreme Brahman;
there is nothing beyond this."
Worshipping him, they said: "You indeed are our father, you who carry us across to the further shore beyond ignorance.
Homage! Homage to the supreme seers! Homage to the supreme seers! (PrUp 6.8)
